questions.prompt: Which country was the first to grant women the national right to vote?
questions.fact: It happened in 1893, though women could not stand for election there for another twenty–six years.

questions.prompt: Who became the first person to travel into space?
questions.fact: The flight lasted 108 minutes, and he was later barred from further missions because he had become too valuable to risk.

questions.prompt: Which US constitutional amendment abolished slavery?
questions.fact: It passed in 1865, though the last state to formally ratify it did not complete the paperwork until 2013.

questions.prompt: Which Roman general crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC?
questions.fact: Bringing an army across that river counted as declaring war on Rome itself, which is why the phrase still means a decision you cannot undo.

questions.prompt: Which 1815 battle ended Napoleon's rule?
questions.fact: It was decided in a single day, and contemporaries noted how close the outcome was for most of the afternoon.

questions.prompt: Which island was Napoleon exiled to after his final defeat?
questions.fact: It sits roughly 1,900 kilometres from the nearest mainland, chosen specifically because escaping it would be far harder than his first exile.

questions.prompt: Which pandemic killed roughly a third of Europe's population in the 1340s?
questions.fact: Labour became so scarce afterwards that wages rose sharply, and several governments passed laws trying to force them back down.

questions.prompt: Which leader founded the largest contiguous land empire in history?
questions.fact: His empire ran a relay postal system across thousands of kilometres, with fresh horses stationed at regular intervals.

questions.prompt: Which ancient Mesopotamian people developed cuneiform writing?
questions.fact: The earliest tablets are overwhelmingly accounting records. Writing appears to have been invented to track grain and livestock.

questions.prompt: Which English monarch reigned when the Spanish Armada was defeated in 1588?
questions.fact: Storms destroyed more of the fleet than the English navy did, on the return voyage around Scotland and Ireland.

questions.prompt: Which US president delivered the Gettysburg Address?
questions.fact: It ran to about two minutes. The speaker before him talked for two hours and is now almost entirely forgotten.

questions.prompt: Which royal dynasty was overthrown in the Russian Revolution of 1917?
questions.fact: They had ruled for just over three hundred years when the last tsar abdicated.

questions.prompt: Which ancient people carved the city of Petra into rock?
questions.fact: They grew wealthy controlling incense trade routes, and built an elaborate system of dams and channels to survive in the desert.

questions.prompt: Which Chinese admiral led vast treasure fleets in the early 1400s?
questions.fact: His largest ships dwarfed anything in contemporary Europe. The voyages were halted by imperial decree and the fleet left to rot.

questions.prompt: The 1969 Stonewall uprising took place in which city?
questions.fact: The first anniversary marches the following year are generally counted as the origin of Pride events worldwide.

questions.prompt: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 ended which conflict?
questions.fact: Historians often date the modern idea of state sovereignty to this settlement, which is why it turns up in international law courses.

questions.prompt: Which English king sealed the Magna Carta in 1215?
questions.fact: The Pope annulled it within ten weeks. It only survived because later kings kept reissuing it to buy support.

questions.prompt: Hadrian's Wall was built by which empire?
questions.fact: It never marked the true edge of the empire. Roman forces operated well north of it for long stretches.

questions.prompt: Which country was known as Persia until 1935?
questions.fact: The name Iran comes from a much older root meaning land of the Aryans, so the change was a return rather than an invention.

questions.prompt: Who led the revolution that made Haiti independent?
questions.fact: It remains the only slave uprising in history that produced a lasting independent state.

questions.prompt: Hannibal famously crossed the Alps to attack which power?
questions.fact: He won nearly every battle in Italy for fifteen years and still lost the war, because he could never take the city itself.

questions.prompt: Which city fell in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire?
questions.fact: Its walls had held off attackers for a thousand years. Large cannon finally made them obsolete in under two months.

questions.prompt: Which conference of 1884 to 1885 carved up Africa among European powers?
questions.fact: No African representatives attended. Many of the resulting straight-line borders are still in place today.

questions.prompt: Which country is named after Simón Bolívar?
questions.fact: He was offered the honour and initially tried to decline it, arguing that naming a country after a living man set a bad precedent.

questions.prompt: Peter the Great founded which city as a new capital?
questions.fact: It was built on marshland at enormous human cost, largely because he wanted a port facing Europe rather than inland Moscow.

questions.prompt: Which civilisation built the stepped pyramid at Chichén Itzá?
questions.fact: On the equinoxes, light and shadow along the staircase produce the shape of a serpent descending the pyramid.

questions.prompt: Which empire recorded information using knotted cords called quipu?
questions.fact: The knots reliably encode numbers. Whether they also carried language is still an open question.

questions.prompt: The Gunpowder Plot of 1605 targeted which building?
questions.fact: The cellars beneath Parliament are still ceremonially searched before each State Opening, four centuries later.

questions.prompt: Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of which kingdom?
questions.fact: Her family was Greek and ruled Egypt for roughly three centuries. She was reportedly the first of them to learn Egyptian.

questions.prompt: Which explorer completed the first circumnavigation of the globe?
questions.fact: Magellan planned the voyage but died partway. Elcano brought one ship and 18 survivors home out of an original 270 men.

questions.prompt: Which ancient library was the largest of the classical world?
questions.fact: There was no single dramatic fire. It declined over centuries through budget cuts, neglect, and repeated damage.

questions.prompt: Which acid gives vinegar its sharp taste?
questions.fact: It is produced by bacteria that convert alcohol, which is why wine left open long enough turns sour on its own.

questions.prompt: Which plant tissue carries water upward from the roots?
questions.fact: There is no pump involved. Water is pulled up by evaporation from the leaves, a chain that can hold together over a hundred metres.

questions.prompt: Which astronomer published the heliocentric model in 1543?
questions.fact: The book appeared in the year he died, which some historians think spared him the controversy that later engulfed Galileo.

questions.prompt: Which organ stores bile produced by the liver?
questions.fact: It can be removed entirely with few lasting effects, since bile simply flows into the intestine continuously instead.

questions.prompt: What are animals without a backbone collectively called?
questions.fact: They account for roughly 95 percent of all known animal species, with beetles alone making up a startling share of that.

questions.prompt: Which scientist discovered penicillin?
questions.fact: He found it by accident on a contaminated dish he had left out, and then struggled for a decade to get anyone interested.

questions.prompt: Which organs filter waste products from the blood?
questions.fact: They process the body's entire blood supply roughly every thirty minutes, filtering around 180 litres of fluid a day.

questions.prompt: Which scale was traditionally used to measure earthquake magnitude?
questions.fact: It is logarithmic, so each whole step represents about thirty times more energy released, not simply one unit more.

questions.prompt: Which metal is the best conductor of electricity?
questions.fact: Copper is used almost everywhere instead, purely because it costs a fraction as much for a barely measurable drop in performance.

questions.prompt: What is a young frog called before it develops legs?
questions.fact: The transformation involves reabsorbing the tail rather than shedding it, recycling the tissue into the developing body.

questions.prompt: Which moon is the largest in the solar system?
questions.fact: It is larger than the planet Mercury, and is the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field.

questions.prompt: Which scientist developed the first widely used polio vaccine?
questions.fact: He declined to patent it, and when asked who owned it replied that the people did, comparing it to owning the Sun.

questions.prompt: What is the centre of an atom called?
questions.fact: It holds nearly all the atom's mass in a tiny fraction of its volume, so matter is overwhelmingly empty space.

questions.prompt: Which process turns a gas directly into a solid without passing through liquid?
questions.fact: Frost forms this way. Water vapour becomes ice on a cold surface without ever pooling as liquid first.

questions.prompt: Which body system includes the heart and blood vessels?
questions.fact: Laid end to end, an adult's blood vessels would wrap around the equator roughly two and a half times.

questions.prompt: Which planet has the strongest winds ever measured in the solar system?
questions.fact: Winds there approach 2,000 km/h, which is strange given it receives roughly a thousandth of the sunlight Earth does.

questions.prompt: Which planet rotates on its side, tipped nearly 98 degrees?
questions.fact: The leading explanation is an ancient collision with something roughly Earth-sized that knocked the whole planet over.

questions.prompt: Which human blood cells have no nucleus when mature?
questions.fact: Ejecting the nucleus frees up space for more haemoglobin. The trade-off is that they cannot repair themselves and last about 120 days.

questions.prompt: Which cell structure carries its own separate DNA?
questions.fact: That DNA is inherited almost entirely from the mother, and it is the main evidence these structures were once free-living bacteria.

questions.prompt: What is absolute zero on the Celsius scale?
questions.fact: It can be approached but never reached. Laboratories have got within a billionth of a degree and no closer.

questions.prompt: Which scientist left gaps in his table to predict elements not yet discovered?
questions.fact: He predicted the properties of gallium and germanium years before anyone found them, and the measurements came back close to his numbers.

questions.prompt: Which animal has the largest brain of any living creature?
questions.fact: It weighs around 7 kilograms, roughly five times a human brain, though brain size alone is a poor guide to intelligence.

questions.prompt: Which force binds protons and neutrons inside an atomic nucleus?
questions.fact: It is the strongest of the four fundamental forces but acts only across distances about the width of a nucleus.

questions.prompt: Which type of rock forms when magma cools and solidifies?
questions.fact: How fast it cools decides the crystal size. Slow cooling underground gives granite; fast cooling at the surface gives basalt.

questions.prompt: Which naturalist independently arrived at natural selection alongside Darwin?
questions.fact: His essay arriving in the post is what finally pushed Darwin, who had sat on the idea for twenty years, into publishing.

questions.prompt: What is a substance that speeds up a reaction without being consumed called?
questions.fact: Nearly every chemical process in your body depends on them. Biological versions are called enzymes.

questions.prompt: Which is the densest planet in the solar system?
questions.fact: Saturn sits at the other extreme. Its average density is below that of water, so it would notionally float given a big enough ocean.

questions.prompt: Which lobe of the brain primarily processes vision?
questions.fact: It sits at the very back of the skull, about as far from the eyes as it is possible to be inside the head.

questions.prompt: What is the term for animals active mainly at dawn and dusk?
questions.fact: Rabbits, deer, and most domestic cats fall into this group, which is why cats often get lively around sunrise and sunset.

questions.prompt: Which process converts a liquid to a gas below its boiling point?
questions.fact: It cools whatever is left behind, because the fastest-moving molecules escape first. That is exactly how sweating works.

questions.prompt: What are the four bases that make up DNA commonly abbreviated as?
questions.fact: The full human sequence runs to about three billion of these pairs, and any two people match across roughly 99.9 percent of them.

questions.prompt: Which two nations compete for the Ashes?
questions.fact: The trophy is a small urn said to contain the ashes of a burnt bail, following a mock obituary for English cricket in 1882.

questions.prompt: How long is an Olympic-standard swimming pool?
questions.fact: Deeper pools produce faster times, because depth reduces the turbulence bouncing back up at the swimmers.

questions.prompt: Which country has won the most Olympic gold medals in total?
questions.fact: Its tally is helped by swimming and athletics, which award far more medals than most other sports on the programme.

questions.prompt: Which sport is contested in a velodrome?
questions.fact: The banking on the steepest bends reaches around 45 degrees, too steep for a rider to remain upright while stationary.

questions.prompt: In cricket, what is a batter dismissed without scoring called?
questions.fact: The term comes from the resemblance between a zero on the scoreboard and a duck's egg.

questions.prompt: The 24 Hours of Le Mans endurance race is held in which country?
questions.fact: Cars cover a distance roughly equivalent to eighteen Formula One races in a single day, with drivers rotating throughout.

questions.prompt: Which martial art and Olympic sport originated in Japan and means gentle way?
questions.fact: Its founder built it around using an opponent's own momentum, which is why size matters less in it than in most combat sports.

questions.prompt: How many rounds are scheduled in a modern professional world title boxing fight?
questions.fact: It was reduced from fifteen in the 1980s after research linked the closing rounds to the most serious injuries.

questions.prompt: Which trophy is contested annually between national teams in men's tennis?
questions.fact: It began in 1900 as a match between the United States and Britain, and now involves well over a hundred nations.

questions.prompt: Which is the oldest of golf's four major championships?
questions.fact: First played in 1860, its trophy is a jug, and winners traditionally keep it only until the following year's tournament.

questions.prompt: In which country did the modern game of golf develop?
questions.fact: Parliament banned it in 1457 because men were playing instead of practising archery, which the crown considered a defence problem.

questions.prompt: Which annual cycling race is the oldest of the sport's three grand tours?
questions.fact: It was invented in 1903 purely as a circulation stunt by a struggling newspaper, and it worked spectacularly.

questions.prompt: The term hat-trick originated in which sport?
questions.fact: A bowler taking three wickets in consecutive deliveries was traditionally rewarded with a hat by his club.

questions.prompt: Which city hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896?
questions.fact: Winners received silver medals, not gold. The gold-silver-bronze arrangement only settled in from 1904.

questions.prompt: How long is a marathon?
questions.fact: The awkward distance was fixed at the 1908 London Games, reportedly so the race could finish in front of the royal box.

questions.prompt: Which colour jersey is worn by the overall leader of the Tour de France?
questions.fact: The colour was chosen to match the yellow newsprint of L'Auto, the newspaper that created the race to sell more copies.

questions.prompt: How many balls are bowled in a standard cricket over?
questions.fact: Australia used eight-ball overs domestically as recently as the 1970s before falling in line with the rest of the game.

questions.prompt: What is the highest possible break in a standard frame of snooker?
questions.fact: A 155 is technically possible but requires the opponent to commit a foul first, and it has never happened in professional competition.

questions.prompt: Which is Canada's official national summer sport?
questions.fact: Canada legislated two national sports in 1994: lacrosse for summer and ice hockey for winter.

questions.prompt: How many players from one team are on a rugby union field at kickoff?
questions.fact: Rugby league split away partly over this. It dropped to thirteen a side to make the game faster and more open.

questions.prompt: Which boxer was universally known as The Greatest?
questions.fact: He was stripped of his title and banned from boxing for over three years at the peak of his career, then came back and regained it.

questions.prompt: Which athlete won four gold medals at the 1936 Berlin Olympics?
questions.fact: A German long jumper reportedly offered him technique advice during the competition, and the two remained friends for life.

questions.prompt: Which country is the birthplace of sumo wrestling?
questions.fact: Many of its rituals come from Shinto practice, which is why salt is thrown into the ring before bouts.

questions.prompt: Which trophy is the oldest in North American professional sport?
questions.fact: It was donated in 1892, predating the league that now awards it by about twenty-five years. Winners' names are engraved directly on it.

questions.prompt: The Kentucky Derby is a race in which sport?
questions.fact: It is nicknamed the most exciting two minutes in sport, because that is roughly how long the race actually lasts.

questions.prompt: Which events make up a triathlon in order?
questions.fact: Swimming goes first for safety. Exhausted swimmers in open water are far more dangerous than exhausted runners on land.

questions.prompt: Which ground is known as the Home of Cricket?
questions.fact: Its playing surface has a noticeable slope, dropping around two and a half metres from one side of the ground to the other.

questions.prompt: How many players from each team are on a basketball court during play?
questions.fact: The game was invented in 1891 using peach baskets, and someone had to retrieve the ball by ladder after every score.

questions.prompt: How many strikes make an out in baseball?
questions.fact: A foul ball counts as a strike, except when it would be the third one, which is why at-bats can run remarkably long.

questions.prompt: In which sport would you compete for the America's Cup?
questions.fact: It is the oldest international trophy in sport, older than the modern Olympics by almost half a century.

questions.prompt: How many players are on the field per side in association football?
questions.fact: Goalkeepers were not required to wear a distinguishing colour until 1909, before which telling them apart was genuinely difficult.

questions.prompt: Which Swedish group released the song Waterloo in 1974?
questions.fact: Winning Eurovision with it launched a career that made the group one of Sweden's most valuable exports for a time.

questions.prompt: Which film is set on the moon Pandora?
questions.fact: Its director waited years to make it, saying the technology needed to film it convincingly did not yet exist.

questions.prompt: Which British band released the album OK Computer?
questions.fact: Much of it was recorded in a historic country mansion, with the band setting up in different rooms for different sounds.

questions.prompt: Which quiz show made the phrase phone a friend famous?
options: Who Wants to Be a Millionaire
questions.fact: The format has been licensed to well over a hundred countries, making it one of television's most exported formats.

questions.prompt: Which comedian voiced Donkey in the Shrek films?
questions.fact: He recorded his lines separately from the other leads, which is common in animation and often surprises audiences.

questions.prompt: Which television series follows a chemistry teacher who begins manufacturing drugs?
questions.fact: The network nearly cancelled it early on, and a writers' strike cut the first season short, which reshaped the whole arc.

questions.prompt: Which band released the album Nevermind?
questions.fact: It knocked Michael Jackson off the top of the US chart in early 1992, a moment often used to date the mainstream arrival of grunge.

questions.prompt: Which director made Inception and Interstellar?
questions.fact: He shoots on film rather than digitally and avoids digital effects where a practical one will do, including building sets that rotate.

questions.prompt: Which South Korean film won the Academy Award for Best Picture?
questions.fact: It was the first film not in English to win the award, in a ceremony held ninety-two years after the first Oscars.

questions.prompt: Which streaming drama chronicles the reign of the British royal family?
questions.fact: The cast was deliberately recast every two seasons so the actors could age with the characters across decades.

questions.prompt: Which 1985 concert raised money for famine relief in Ethiopia?
questions.fact: It was broadcast to an estimated 1.5 billion viewers across more than a hundred countries, using satellite links that had never been attempted at that scale.

questions.prompt: Which musical by Lin-Manuel Miranda tells the story of a US founding father?
questions.fact: He began writing it after picking up a biography to read on holiday, expecting it to be a relaxing beach book.

questions.prompt: Which comedian co-created Seinfeld?
questions.fact: The pilot tested so poorly with audiences that the network initially ordered only four more episodes.

questions.prompt: Which horror film franchise features the character Michael Myers?
questions.fact: The mask was a cheap Star Trek Captain Kirk mask, bought for under two dollars and painted white by the crew.

questions.prompt: Which studio produced Toy Story, the first fully computer-animated feature film?
questions.fact: The studio began as a computer hardware division and only moved into films after the hardware business struggled.

questions.prompt: Which album is the best-selling of all time?
options: The Dark Side of the Moon
questions.fact: Its title track's video ran fourteen minutes, long enough that it was screened in cinemas to qualify for an Academy Award.

questions.prompt: In which television series do characters meet at Central Perk?
questions.fact: The six leads negotiated their salaries collectively rather than individually, which was almost unheard of in television at the time.

questions.prompt: Which director made Pulp Fiction?
questions.fact: He wrote much of it while working in a video rental shop, where he had watched an enormous number of films on the job.

questions.prompt: Which film features the character Vito Corleone?
questions.fact: The studio fought hard against casting Marlon Brando, who had to audition on tape despite already being a major star.

questions.prompt: Which awards honour achievement in American television?
questions.fact: Winning one in all four major American entertainment award categories is known as an EGOT, and fewer than twenty people have done it.

questions.prompt: Which musician was known as the King of Rock and Roll?
questions.fact: He never performed a full concert outside North America, despite being one of the most globally recognised performers of his era.

questions.prompt: Which Indian film industry takes its name from Bombay?
questions.fact: India releases more feature films per year than any other country, by a wide margin.

questions.prompt: Which reggae artist recorded No Woman, No Cry?
questions.fact: The songwriting credit went to a friend who ran a Kingston soup kitchen, reportedly so the royalties would keep it running.

questions.prompt: Which streaming service released House of Cards as an early flagship original?
questions.fact: Releasing an entire season at once was a deliberate break from weekly scheduling, and it effectively invented modern binge-watching.

questions.prompt: Which actor played Wolverine across nearly two decades of films?
questions.fact: He was cast only weeks into filming after the original actor dropped out, and had not read the comics beforehand.

questions.prompt: Which fashion house did Coco Chanel found?
questions.fact: She started as a hat maker. The move into clothing came from using jersey fabric, then considered suitable only for underwear.

questions.prompt: Which singer is nicknamed the Material Girl?
questions.fact: She has said she came to dislike the nickname, since the song was intended as satire rather than a personal statement.

questions.prompt: Which board game involves buying and trading properties?
questions.fact: An earlier version was designed to demonstrate how rent extraction concentrates wealth, which is close to the opposite of how it is played.

questions.prompt: Which video game character is a plumber created by Nintendo?
questions.fact: The moustache and cap exist for technical reasons. Early hardware could not render a mouth or hair clearly at that resolution.

questions.prompt: Which annual music festival is held in the California desert at Indio?
questions.fact: It grew out of a single 1993 protest concert staged at the site by a band boycotting a nearby venue.

questions.prompt: Which South Korean group released the English-language single Dynamite?
questions.fact: It was their first single recorded entirely in English, released during a year when touring was impossible.

questions.prompt: Which sea separates the Arabian Peninsula from northeast Africa?
questions.fact: It is widening by about a centimetre a year as the plates on either side pull apart, and will eventually become an ocean.

questions.prompt: Which Central American country abolished its standing army in 1948?
questions.fact: The military budget was redirected largely into education and healthcare, and the policy has held for over seventy-five years.

questions.prompt: Which city is traditionally known as the Eternal City?
questions.fact: It contains an entire sovereign state within its boundaries, which no other city in the world can claim.

questions.prompt: Which country has the largest population in Africa?
questions.fact: More than five hundred languages are spoken within its borders, one of the highest counts of any country on Earth.

questions.prompt: Which body of water lies between Great Britain and Ireland?
questions.fact: At its narrowest the crossing is around 20 kilometres, and on clear days each coast is plainly visible from the other.

questions.prompt: Which river flows through Baghdad?
questions.fact: Together with the Euphrates it defined Mesopotamia, a name that simply means the land between the rivers.

questions.prompt: Which European capital was formed by merging Buda and Pest?
questions.fact: The two sides were only joined by a permanent bridge in 1849, and unified into one city a quarter century later.

questions.prompt: Which lake holds the most fresh water and is the deepest in the world?
questions.fact: It contains roughly a fifth of all unfrozen fresh water on the planet, more than all five North American Great Lakes together.

questions.prompt: Which sea lies between Italy and the Balkan peninsula?
questions.fact: Venice sits at its northern end, and the city's long dominance of its trade routes is why it grew so wealthy.

questions.prompt: Which is the northernmost capital city of a sovereign state?
questions.fact: Almost all of its heating and electricity comes from geothermal and hydroelectric sources, thanks to the volcanic ground beneath it.

questions.prompt: Which desert spans much of Botswana and Namibia?
questions.fact: It receives too much rainfall to be a true desert by strict definition, and supports far more vegetation than most people expect.

questions.prompt: Which African country is almost entirely enclosed by Senegal?
questions.fact: Its borders follow a river, and the country is barely fifty kilometres wide at its broadest point.

questions.prompt: Which plateau is known as the roof of the world?
questions.fact: Most of Asia's major rivers rise there, which is why it is sometimes called the water tower of the continent.

questions.prompt: Which Moroccan city is known for its large historic medina and souks?
questions.fact: The old walled quarter is largely closed to cars, and its street layout has changed remarkably little in eight centuries.

questions.prompt: Which mountain sits on the border between Nepal and Tibet?
questions.fact: It grows by roughly four millimetres a year as the Indian plate continues pushing north into Asia.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest desert in the world?
questions.fact: Deserts are defined by how little precipitation they receive, not by heat, which is why the coldest place on Earth qualifies.

questions.prompt: Which mountain is the tallest when measured from its base rather than sea level?
questions.fact: Measured from its base on the ocean floor it exceeds 10,000 metres, comfortably beating Everest, but most of it is underwater.

questions.prompt: Which sea has no coastline?
questions.fact: It is bounded entirely by ocean currents rather than land, and European eels cross the Atlantic to spawn there.

questions.prompt: Which is the deepest known point in the ocean?
questions.fact: Drop Everest into it and the peak would still sit more than two kilometres below the surface.

questions.prompt: Which country is nicknamed the Land of Fire and Ice?
questions.fact: It sits on the boundary of two tectonic plates, which are pulling apart at roughly the rate fingernails grow.

questions.prompt: Which country's name comes from the Spanish word for equator?
questions.fact: Because the planet bulges at the equator, its highest peak's summit is the furthest point from the centre of the Earth.

questions.prompt: Which is the driest non-polar desert on Earth?
questions.fact: Some weather stations there have never recorded rainfall, and the terrain is used to test equipment bound for Mars.

questions.prompt: Which archipelago nation is made up of more than 7,000 islands?
questions.fact: Only around 2,000 of them are inhabited, and several hundred still do not have official names.

questions.prompt: Which mountain range is traditionally taken as the boundary between Europe and Asia?
questions.fact: They are among the oldest mountains on the planet, which is why they are comparatively low and heavily worn down.

questions.prompt: Which country was formerly known as Ceylon?
questions.fact: The name change came in 1972, though the old name survives commercially on tea packaging to this day.

questions.prompt: Which is the highest uninterrupted waterfall in the world?
questions.fact: It is so tall that in the dry season much of the water evaporates or blows away before reaching the bottom.

questions.prompt: Which lake is so salty that swimmers float without effort?
questions.fact: Its shoreline is the lowest exposed land on Earth, sitting more than 400 metres below sea level and still dropping.

questions.prompt: Which country holds the largest share of the Amazon rainforest?
questions.fact: The forest generates much of its own rainfall, with moisture recycled through the canopy several times on its way inland.

questions.prompt: Which is the highest administrative capital city in the world?
questions.fact: It sits above 3,600 metres, thin enough air that visiting football teams have long complained about playing there.

questions.prompt: Which country contains the Southern Alps?
questions.fact: The range is still rising by roughly a centimetre a year, though erosion removes almost as much as the uplift adds.

questions.prompt: Which country officially spans the most time zones?
questions.fact: Counting its overseas territories it covers twelve, more than Russia. China, despite its width, uses only one.

questions.prompt: How many lines does a sonnet have?
questions.fact: The Italian and English forms split those lines differently, which changes where the argument of the poem is allowed to turn.

questions.prompt: Which Dickens novel features the convict Magwitch?
questions.fact: Dickens rewrote the ending after a friend objected, replacing a bleaker original with something more hopeful.

questions.prompt: Which literary device repeats initial consonant sounds in nearby words?
questions.fact: Old English poetry used it structurally rather than decoratively, taking the place that rhyme holds in later verse.

questions.prompt: Which novel opens with the words It was the best of times?
questions.fact: That opening sentence runs to well over a hundred words before it reaches a full stop.

questions.prompt: Which Japanese poetic form has three lines of five, seven, and five syllables?
questions.fact: Traditional examples nearly always reference a season, often through a single conventional word.

questions.prompt: Which novel follows the Joad family west during the Dust Bowl?
questions.fact: It was publicly burned and banned in parts of California, where local authorities disputed its portrayal of migrant conditions.

questions.prompt: Which Shakespeare tragedy is set largely in Verona?
questions.fact: The entire action covers only about four days, which is part of why the events feel so headlong.

questions.prompt: Which Irish author wrote Ulysses?
questions.fact: The whole novel takes place across a single day in Dublin, 16 June 1904, still marked annually as Bloomsday.

questions.prompt: Which novel is narrated by a butler reflecting on his years of service?
questions.fact: Its author has said he wrote it in roughly four weeks of deliberately isolated, uninterrupted work.

questions.prompt: Which Greek tragedy ends with a king blinding himself?
questions.fact: Aristotle used it as his central example of tragic structure, which is much of why it dominates drama syllabuses.

questions.prompt: Which poem begins Two roads diverged in a yellow wood?
questions.fact: It is widely read as a celebration of individualism, though the poet described it as a gently ironic joke about indecision.

questions.prompt: Which ancient epic follows a Mesopotamian king and his companion Enkidu?
questions.fact: It survives on clay tablets and includes a flood narrative that predates the biblical version by centuries.

questions.prompt: Which Brontë novel is set on the Yorkshire moors?
questions.fact: Early reviewers found it brutal and strange, and it was long treated as the lesser sister novel before its reputation reversed.

questions.prompt: Which Jane Austen novel centres on a matchmaker named Emma Woodhouse?
questions.fact: Austen reportedly said she was taking on a heroine whom no one but herself would much like.

questions.prompt: Which novel is written as a series of letters from a woman named Celie?
questions.fact: It won both the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award, and has been among the most frequently challenged books in US schools.

questions.prompt: Which Greek playwright wrote Antigone?
questions.fact: He wrote well over a hundred plays and only seven survive complete, which is roughly the survival rate for Greek drama overall.

questions.prompt: Which novel features a woman forced to wear a scarlet letter A?
questions.fact: Its long opening chapter about a customs house has almost nothing to do with the plot and was added to pad the length.

questions.prompt: What is a long narrative poem recounting heroic deeds called?
questions.fact: The oldest examples were composed to be performed aloud from memory, which is why they lean so heavily on repeated phrases.

questions.prompt: Which Russian novel opens with a famous line about happy families?
questions.fact: Its author later dismissed his own great novels as trivial, having undergone a severe religious and moral crisis.

questions.prompt: Which literary device gives human qualities to objects or animals?
questions.fact: Fables depend on it almost entirely, which is why talking animals feel natural in stories aimed at teaching a lesson.

questions.prompt: In Hamlet, who murders the prince's father?
questions.fact: At roughly 4,000 lines it is Shakespeare's longest play, and is rarely performed uncut.

questions.prompt: Which novel features the character Bigger Thomas?
options: Go Tell It on the Mountain
questions.fact: It was among the first books by a Black American author selected by the Book of the Month Club, which made it a national bestseller.

questions.prompt: Which term describes a story with a hidden moral or political meaning?
questions.fact: Writers under censorship have relied on it heavily, since a story about animals or islands can say what a direct essay cannot.

questions.prompt: Which novel features a character called Offred?
questions.fact: The name is not a name at all. It marks her as belonging to a man called Fred, which is the point of it.

questions.prompt: Which epic poem follows Odysseus on his journey home?
questions.fact: The word odyssey entered English as a common noun only in the 1880s, borrowed straight from the poem's title.

questions.prompt: Which novel opens with a dream of a house called Manderley?
questions.fact: The narrator is never given a first name anywhere in the book, a detail most readers only notice on reflection.

questions.prompt: Who wrote Wide Sargasso Sea, a response to an earlier English novel?
questions.fact: It retells Jane Eyre from the perspective of the first wife, and was published nearly 120 years after the original.

questions.prompt: Which Belgian detective did Agatha Christie create?
questions.fact: He is the only fictional character to have received a front-page obituary in The New York Times.

questions.prompt: Which Nigerian writer won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986?
questions.fact: He was the first African laureate in literature, and had earlier spent two years imprisoned largely in solitary confinement.

questions.prompt: Which Chilean poet won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971?
questions.fact: Pablo Neruda was a pen name. He adopted it as a teenager, partly to keep his father from discovering he wrote poetry.

questions.prompt: Who wrote the dystopian novel featuring the Thought Police?
questions.fact: He finished it while seriously ill on a remote Scottish island, typing the final draft himself in bed.

questions.prompt: What is a CAPTCHA designed to determine?
questions.fact: Early versions doubled as free labour, using the answers to digitise words that scanning software had failed to read from old books.

questions.prompt: Which company publishes the Ubuntu operating system?
questions.fact: The name comes from a southern African concept usually translated as humanity toward others.

questions.prompt: Which technology underlies cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin?
questions.fact: The design solves the problem of agreeing on a shared record without anyone in charge, which is harder than the cryptography involved.

questions.prompt: Which wireless standard is used for short-range device pairing?
questions.fact: It is named after a tenth-century Danish king, and its logo combines the runes for his initials.

questions.prompt: Which company develops the Photoshop image editing software?
questions.fact: It was written by two brothers, one of whom went on to work in visual effects at Industrial Light and Magic.

questions.prompt: What does the term phishing describe?
questions.fact: The unusual spelling traces back to phone phreaking, an earlier culture of exploring and exploiting telephone systems.

questions.prompt: Which satellite navigation system is operated by the European Union?
questions.fact: It was built partly so Europe would not depend on a system controlled by another government's military.

questions.prompt: What is a network of compromised computers controlled remotely called?
questions.fact: Owners usually have no idea their machine is part of one, since the software is designed to stay quiet and use spare capacity.

questions.prompt: Which company designs the graphics processors most widely used to train AI models?
questions.fact: The chips were built for rendering game graphics. Their usefulness for AI came from the same ability to do many simple calculations at once.

questions.prompt: Which company owns Instagram?
questions.fact: It was bought in 2012 for about a billion dollars when it had thirteen employees and no revenue.

questions.prompt: What does a firewall do on a computer network?
questions.fact: The name is borrowed from building construction, where a fire wall is a physical barrier meant to stop a fire spreading between sections.

questions.prompt: Which machine was built at Bletchley Park to break German codes?
questions.fact: Most of them were dismantled after the war and the work stayed secret for decades, so its designers received no public credit at the time.

questions.prompt: Which type of computer memory keeps its contents without power?
questions.fact: Flash storage works by trapping electrons in an insulated layer, which is also why it eventually wears out after enough write cycles.

questions.prompt: Which company manufactures the majority of the world's most advanced chips?
questions.fact: It builds chips designed by other companies rather than selling its own, a model that barely existed before it proved it could work.

questions.prompt: Which search engine was founded by two Stanford graduate students in 1998?
questions.fact: They tried to sell the technology early on for around a million dollars, and could not find a buyer willing to pay it.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym VR stand for in computing?
questions.fact: Working head-mounted displays date to the 1960s. One early rig was so heavy it had to be suspended from the ceiling.

questions.prompt: Which key on a standard keyboard is the widest?
questions.fact: The QWERTY arrangement around it was designed for mechanical typewriters, and survives purely because retraining everyone was never worth it.

questions.prompt: Who is widely regarded as the first computer programmer?
questions.fact: Her notes on a machine that was never built describe how it could handle symbols rather than only numbers.

questions.prompt: What was the first message ever sent over ARPANET?
questions.fact: They were typing LOGIN and the system crashed after two characters, making the accidental first word LO.

questions.prompt: Which operating system kernel did Linus Torvalds create?
questions.fact: He announced it as a hobby project that would not be big and professional, and it now runs most of the world's servers.

questions.prompt: Who co-founded Apple alongside Steve Jobs?
questions.fact: A third founder sold his 10 percent stake for 800 dollars less than two weeks in.

questions.prompt: In computing, where does the term bug reportedly come from?
options: A moth found in a relay
questions.fact: The moth was taped into a logbook in 1947 with the note that it was the first actual case of a bug being found.

questions.prompt: What does DNS do on the internet?
options: Translates domain names to IP addresses
questions.fact: Without it the web would still work, but you would have to remember a string of numbers for every site you visit.

questions.prompt: Which test for machine intelligence is named after a British mathematician?
questions.fact: He framed it as an imitation game, sidestepping the question of whether a machine thinks in favour of whether it can convince you.

questions.prompt: Which number base does the binary system use?
questions.fact: Computers use it because a circuit only has to distinguish between on and off, which is far more reliable than ten voltage levels.

questions.prompt: Which company created the Game Boy?
questions.fact: Its screen was deliberately low-tech so the batteries would last, and it outsold more powerful colour rivals for years.

questions.prompt: Which company designs the processor architecture used in most smartphones?
questions.fact: It manufactures almost nothing itself. The business is licensing designs, which is why its architecture is nearly everywhere.

questions.prompt: What is a self-replicating program that spreads across networks called?
questions.fact: The first widely known one in 1988 was meant to measure the size of the internet, and accidentally took down much of it.

questions.prompt: Which protocol suite underpins how data moves across the internet?
questions.fact: It breaks every message into packets that can travel separate routes and be reassembled in the right order at the other end.

questions.prompt: Which storage format held 1.44 megabytes and was standard into the 1990s?
questions.fact: Its shape survives as the save icon in software written for people who have never handled one.

questions.prompt: Which social network was launched from a Harvard dorm room in 2004?
questions.fact: It required a university email address for its first two years, which is much of why it spread campus by campus.
